source_text: Aut optimum est hic retineri, secundum aoros; aut pessimum, secundum biaeothanatos, ut ipsis jam vocabulis utar, quibus auctrix opinionum istarum magia sonat, Hostanes et Typhon, et Dardanus, et Damigeron, et Nectabis, et Berenice. Publica jam literatura est, quae animas etiam justa aetate sopitas, etiam proba morte disjunctas, etiam prompta humatione dispunctas, evocaturam se ab inferum incolatu pollicetur. Quid ergo dicemus magiam? Quod omnes pene: fallaciam. Sed ratio fallaciae solos non fugit Christianos, qui spiritalia nequitiae, non quidem socia conscientia, sed inimica scientia novimus, nec invitatoria operatione, sed expugnatoria dominatione tractamus; multiformem luem mentis humanae, totius erroris artificem, salutis pariter animaeque vastatricem scientiam magiae, secundae scilicet idololatriae, in qua se daemones perinde mortuos fingunt, quemadmodum in illa deos. Quidni? cum et dii mortui. Itaque invocantur quidem aori et biaeothanati, sub illo fidei argumento, quod credibile videatur eas potissimum animas ad vim et injuriam facere, quas per vim et saevus et immaturus finis extorsit, quasi ad vicem offensae. Sed daemones operantur sub obtentu earum; et hi vel maxime, qui in ipsis tunc fuerunt cum adviverent, quique illas in hujusmodi impegerunt exitus. Nam, et suggessimus nullum pene hominem carere daemonio, et pluribus notum est daemoniorum quoque opera et immaturas et atroces effici mortes, quas incursibus deputant. Hanc quoque fallaciam spiritus nequam sub personis defunctorum delitescentis, nisi fallor, etiam rebus probamus, cum in exorcismis interdum aliquem se ex parentibus hominem suis affirmat, interdum gladiatorem, vel bestiarium, sicut et alibi deum; nihil magis curans, quam hoc ipsum excludere quod praedicamus, ne facile credamus animas universas ad inferos redigi, ut et judicii et resurrectionis fidem turbet. Et tamen ille daemon postquam circumstantes circumvenire tentavit, instantia divinae gratiae victus, id quod in vero est, invitus confitetur. Sic et in illa alia specie magiae, quae jam quiescentes animas evellere ab inferis creditur et conspectui exhibere, non alia fallaciae vis est operatior. Plane quia et phantasma praestatur, quia et corpus adfingitur; nec magnum illi exteriores oculos circumscribere, cui interiorem mentis aciem excaecare perfacile est. Corpora denique videbantur Pharaoni et Aegyptiis magicarum virgarum dracones, sed Moysi veritas mendacium devoravit. Multa utique et adversus Apostolos Simon dedit, et Elymas magi; sed plaga caecitatis de praestigiis non fuit. Quid novi aemulatio veritatis a spiritu immundo? Ecce hodie ejusdem Simonis haereticos tanta praesumptio artis extollit, ut etiam prophetarum animas ab inferis movere se spondeant. Et credo quia mendacio possunt; nec enim pythonico tunc spiritui minus licuit animam Samuelis effingere, post Deum mortuos consulente Saule. Absit alioquin ut animam cujuslibet sancti, nedum prophetae, a daemonio credamus extractam, edocti quod ipse Satanas transfiguretur in angelum lucis, nedum in hominem lucis, etiam deum se adseveraturus in fine, signaque portentosiora editurus, ad evertendos, si fieri possit, electos. Dubitavit, si forte, tunc prophetam se Dei asseverare, et utique Sauli, in quo jam ipse morabatur? Ne putes alium fuisse qui phantasma administrabat, alium qui commendabat; sed eumdem spiritum, et in pseudoprophetide, et in apostata facile mentiri, quod fecerat credi, per quem Saulis thesaurus illic erat, ubi et cor ipsius, ubi scilicet Deus non erat. Et ideo per quem visurum se credidit, vidit; quia per quem vidit, et credidit. Si et de nocturnis imaginibus opponitur, saepe non frustra mortuos visos (nam et Nasammonas propria oracula apud parentum sepulchra mansitando captare, ut Heraclides scribit, vel Nymphodorus, vel Herodotus; et Celtas apud virorum fortium busta eadem de caussa abnoctare, ut Nicander affirmat), non magis mortuos vere patimur in somnis, quam vivos, sed eadem ratione mortuos qua et vivos, et omnia quae videntur. Non enim quia videntur, vera sunt, sed quia adimplentur. Fides somniorum de effectu, non de conspectu renuntiatur. Nulli autem animae omnino inferos patere, satis Dominus in argumento illo pauperis requiescentis, et divitis ingemiscentis, ex persona Abrahae sanxit, non posse inde relegari renuntiatorem dispositionis infernae; quod vel tunc licere potuisset, ut Moysi et Prophetis crederetur. Sed etsi quasdam revocavit in corpora Dei virtus, in documenta juris sui, non idcirco communicabitur fidei, et audaciae magorum, et fallaciae somniorum, et licentiae poetarum. Atquin in resurrectionis exemplis, cum Dei virtus, sive per Prophetas, sive per Christum, sive per Apostolos in corpora animas repraesentat, solida et contrectabili, et satiata veritate, praejudicatum est hanc esse formam veritatis, ut omnem mortuorum exhibitionem incorporalem praestigias judices.
pass_a_gloss: Or it is best to be retained here, according to the aoros; or it is worst, according to the biaeothanatos, so that we use the very words by which the magia, the author of these opinions, sounds, Hostanes and Typhon, and Dardanus, and Damigeron, and Nectabis, and Berenice. Now the public literature is, which promises that it will evoke the souls even of the just age, even of the good death, even of the prompt burial, from the infernal dwelling. What therefore shall we say about magia? That almost all: deceit. But the reason of deceit does not flee only the Christians, who know the spiritual wickedness, not as a companion of conscience, but as an enemy of knowledge, and we treat it not with inviting operation, but with expugnatorial domination; the multiform plague of the human mind, the artisan of all error, the devastator of the salvation and of the soul, the knowledge of magia, namely the second idolatry, in which the demons feign themselves to be dead, just as in that one they feign themselves to be gods. Why not? since even the gods are dead. And so the aori and the biaeothanati are invoked, under that argument of faith, which seems credible that those souls especially are forced to violence and injury, which were torn away by violence and by savage and immature end, as if in revenge for the offense. But the demons operate under the pretext of them; and these especially, who were in them when they were alive, and who drove them to such exits. For we have suggested that almost no man is without a demon, and it is known to many that the works of demons also effect immature and atrocious deaths, which they attribute to their attacks. We also prove this deceit of the evil spirit hiding under the persons of the dead, unless I am mistaken, by the facts, when in exorcisms sometimes it affirms itself to be a man from the parents, sometimes a gladiator, or a bestiarius, just as also elsewhere a god; nothing caring more than to exclude this very thing which we preach, so that we may not easily believe that all souls are reduced to the infernos, so that it may disturb the faith of the judgment and of the resurrection. And yet that demon, after trying to deceive those standing around, was defeated by the instance of divine grace, and confessed, unwillingly, what is true. So also in that other species of magia, which is believed to evoke the resting souls from the infernos and to exhibit them to sight, there is not another force of deceit operating. Clearly, because also a phantasm is provided, because also a body is feigned; and it is not great for him to deceive the external eyes, to whom it is easy to blind the internal aim of the mind. Finally, the bodies of the dragons of the magical wands were seen by Pharaoh and the Egyptians, but the truth of Moses devoured the lie. Many things were also given by Simon against the Apostles, and by Elymas the magician; but the plague of blindness was not from the prestidigitation. What is new, the emulation of truth by the unclean spirit? Behold, today the heretics of the same Simon are lifted up by so great a presumption of art, that they even promise to move the souls of the prophets from the infernos. And I believe that they can do it by lie; for it was not less permitted to the pythonic spirit then to feign the soul of Samuel, after God, consulting the dead Saul. Let it be absent otherwise, that we believe any soul of a saint, nay, of a prophet, to be extracted by a demon, taught that Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light, nay, into a man of light, and even into a god, asserting himself, and editing portentous signs, to subvert, if it is possible, the elect. Did he doubt, if perhaps, then to assert himself to be a prophet of God, and certainly to Saul, in whom he himself was dwelling? Do not think that there was another who administered the phantasm, another who commended; but the same spirit, and in the pseudoprophet, and in the apostate, easily lied, what he made to be believed, through whom the treasure of Saul was there, where also his heart was, where certainly God was not. And therefore, through whom he believed himself to see, he saw; because through whom he saw, he also believed. If also the nocturnal images are opposed, often not in vain the dead are seen (for also the Nasammones, as Heraclides writes, or Nymphodorus, or Herodotus, stayed near the sepulchres of their parents, capturing their own oracles; and the Celts, as Nicander affirms, stayed near the busts of strong men for the same reason), we do not suffer the dead in dreams more truly than the living, but for the same reason the dead as the living, and all things which are seen. For they are not true because they are seen, but because they are fulfilled. The faith of dreams is announced from the effect, not from the sight. However, no soul at all suffers the infernos, as the Lord sanctioned in that argument of the resting poor man, and of the groaning rich man, from the person of Abraham, announcing that it is not possible to be sent back from there as a renouncer of the disposition of the infernos; which would have been possible even then, so that it might be believed by Moses and the Prophets. But even if the virtue of God has recalled some into bodies, as documents of his law, it will not be communicated to the faith, and to the audacity of the magicians, and to the deceit of dreams, and to the license of the poets. But in the examples of the resurrection, when the virtue of God, either through the Prophets, or through Christ, or through the Apostles, represents the souls in bodies, solid and tangible, and satisfied with truth, it is prejudged that this is the form of truth, so that every exhibition of the dead is judged to be incorporal prestidigitation.

pass_b_english: It is best to stay here, according to the *aoroi*; or worst, according to the *biaeothanatoi* — borrowing the very terms by which the *magia* that authored these opinions makes its noise: Hostanes, Typhon, Dardanus, Damigeron, Nectabis, Berenice. Public literature now promises to evoke souls from the infernal dwelling — souls settled at a just age, severed by a good death, dispatched with prompt burial. So what shall we call *magia*? What almost everyone does: a fraud. But the logic of the fraud escapes only Christians. We know the spiritual wickedness not as a conscience's companion but as knowledge's enemy, and we engage it not with inviting operation but with storming domination: the multiform plague of the human mind, the artisan of all error, the devastator alike of salvation and soul — the knowledge of *magia*, that is, second idolatry, in which demons feign themselves dead just as in the first they feigned themselves gods. Why not? Since the gods themselves are dead.

Hence *aoroi* and *biaeothanatoi* are invoked on the credible-sounding argument that souls wrenched by violent, savage, immature ends are especially forced to violence and injury — as if in revenge for the offense. But demons operate under cover of those souls; above all the demons who already dwelt in them while they lived and who drove them to such exits. For we have shown that almost no human lacks a demon, and many know that demonic operations also produce immature and atrocious deaths, which get blamed on attacks. We prove, too, this fraud of the evil spirit hiding under the persons of the dead: in exorcisms a demon sometimes claims to be a man from his parents, sometimes a gladiator or a *bestiarius*, elsewhere a god — caring nothing more than to exclude the very thing we preach, so that we will not easily believe all souls are dragged to the infernal regions and so disturb the faith of the judgment and the resurrection. Yet that demon, after trying to deceive the bystanders, was conquered by the instance of divine grace and confessed the truth against its will.

So also in that other species of *magia*, which claims to evoke resting souls from the infernos and exhibit them to sight, no different force of fraud is at work. Plainly: a phantasm is supplied, a body feigned; and it is no great feat to deceive external eyes for one to whom blinding the mind's inner aim is effortless. Finally, Pharaoh and the Egyptians saw the bodies of the magical wands' dragons, but Moses' truth devoured the lie. Simon and the magician Elymas also threw much against the Apostles; but the plague of blindness was no sleight of hand. What is new about the unclean spirit's emulation of truth? Behold, today the heretics of that same Simon are lifted by so great a presumption of art that they even promise to move the souls of the prophets from the infernos. And I believe they can do it by a lie; for the pythonic spirit was no less permitted to feign Samuel's soul when Saul consulted the dead after God (Luke 16:19-31). Far be it otherwise that we believe any saint's soul, let alone a prophet's, extracted by a demon — taught that Satan himself transforms into an angel of light, nay, into a man of light, and will even assert himself a god and produce portentous signs to subvert, if possible, the elect.

Did he perhaps doubt then to assert himself a prophet of God, and certainly to Saul, in whom he was already dwelling? Do not suppose one spirit administered the phantasm and another commended it; it was the same spirit, lying easily both in the pseudoprophetess and in the apostate, making believed what he had caused to be believed — he through whom Saul's treasure was where his heart was, where God certainly was not. And therefore through whom he believed he would see, he saw; because through whom he saw, he also believed. If nocturnal images are also opposed: the dead are often seen in dreams not in vain (for the Nasammones, as Heraclides writes, or Nymphodorus, or Herodotus, stayed by their parents' tombs capturing oracles; and the Celts, as Nicander affirms, kept vigil by the tombs of strong men for the same reason). We do not experience the dead in dreams any more truly than the living, but by the same reason the dead as the living, and all things that appear. For they are not true because they are seen, but because they are fulfilled. The faith of dreams is declared from the effect, not from the sight.

But no soul at all has the infernos open to it: the Lord sanctioned this in that parable of the resting poor man and the groaning rich man, from the person of Abraham, declaring it impossible for a renouncer of the infernal disposition to be sent back from there — which would have been possible even then, so that they might believe Moses and the Prophets (Luke 16:19-31). Even if God's power has recalled some into bodies as documents of his law, that will not be conceded to the faith, the audacity of magicians, the fraud of dreams, or the license of poets. But in the resurrection examples, when God's power — whether through Prophets, or through Christ, or through Apostles — represents souls in bodies solid, tangible, and satisfied with truth, it is prejudged that this is the form of truth, so that every incorporeal exhibition of the dead is judged mere prestidigitation.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments regarding magic, demons, and the state of the dead. Scripture citations (Luke 16:19-31) correctly identify the alluded parable of Abraham, Lazarus, and the rich man. The distinction between 'aoros' and 'biaeothanatos' as technical terms is preserved. Pass A and B are consistent with the Latin source.
